rationale: A wins because it keeps the story interesting without inflating the facts past recognition. Its “Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank” angle is usefully uncomfortable and immediately names the proof required. B has usable bones, but “The bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built is becoming a mass-market consumer bank” is a factual bruise in the headline: Mercury is not a chartered bank, the product is invite-only, and the banking services run through partners.
gaps_in_A: “The launch is live today” is a touch more declarative than the supplied facts. The update says Mercury is launching at a timestamp; it does not explicitly say accounts are already live.

“Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank” is strong, but legally imprecise. The update says partner banks provide the banking services, so the angle needs to keep custody language exact.

The set rightly asks “Who actually gets invites first?” but does not turn that into a conditional distribution angle. If existing business customers get first access, that may be the sharper business story.
gaps_in_B: “The bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built is becoming a mass-market consumer bank” stacks three overclaims in one headline. Mercury is not a bank, the update says invite-only with a waitlist, and “mass-market” is not supported.
“well-capitalized, previously B2B-only player” invents capital position from thin air. Profitable is not the same as well-capitalized, and the update gives no balance-sheet detail.
“the notoriously thin margins of consumer banking” may be true industry context, but it is not in the supplied facts. As written, B treats outside analysis as established evidence.

“When a business-only fintech decides it's ready to be a full-service bank” is padded category bait. Checking and savings through partner banks do not make Mercury a full-service bank, and the angle admits it is “one company, not yet a confirmed pattern.”
